1.q: וַֽ⁠יְהִי֙ בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת שָׁלֹ֔שׁ לְ⁠הוֹשֵׁ֥עַ בֶּן־אֵלָ֖ה מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל מָלַ֛ךְ חִזְקִיָּ֥ה בֶן־אָחָ֖ז מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה
1.note: In this verse and the next two verses, the author is introducing **Hezekiah** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Judah**. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar expressions in 8:16. (In this instance, the author uses the phrase **And it happened** to introduce a participant. He may do this to highlight the exceptional godly character of Hezekiah. Consider how you have been translating that phrase and how you might express its meaning here.)
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:25. Alternate translation: [in the third year of Hoshea]

2.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:17. Alternate translation: [He was 25 years old]

3.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:13. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh considered to be right]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:24. Alternate translation: [his ancestor]

4.note: The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he removed** already includes this meaning. He may be doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what Hezekiah did and what previous kings had done, even godly ones such as Joash, Azariah, and Jotham. The author notes that those kings “did right in the eyes of Yahweh,” but even so, “the high places were not removed.” Alternate translation: [Unlike previous kings, he removed]

This could be a reference to: (1) many different Asherah poles that the Judeans had set up throughout their kingdom. The word **Asherah** is singular in form, but it would be referring to all of these poles as a group. Alternate translation: [all of the Asherah poles that people had set up] or (2) a specific prominent Asherah pole, such as the one the author describes in 13:6. If so, it would have been in Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [the prominent Asherah pole in Jerusalem]

4.q: וְ⁠כִתַּת֩ נְחַ֨שׁ הַ⁠נְּחֹ֜שֶׁת אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֣ה מֹשֶׁ֗ה כִּ֣י עַד־הַ⁠יָּמִ֤ים הָ⁠הֵ֨מָּה֙ הָי֤וּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מְקַטְּרִ֣ים ל֔⁠וֹ וַ⁠יִּקְרָא־ל֖⁠וֹ נְחֻשְׁתָּֽן
4.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because until those days the sons of Israel were offering incense to the serpent of bronze that Moses had made (and one called it Nehushtan), he broke it up]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:6. Alternate translation: [that time]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:12. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

Here the author is using the pronoun **one** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and it was called Nehushtan] or [and it had come to be called Nehushtan]

5.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 17:2. Alternate translation: [nor those who were before him]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [, nor had any of those who were before him been like him]

6.note: The author is speaking of Hezekiah continually being loyal to Yahweh as if he had **clung** to him physically. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he was loyal to Yahweh continually]

The author is speaking as if Hezekiah had been following Yahweh down a path and as if he could have **turned away** from him physically. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he did not stop obeying him]
In some languages it may be more natural to use the name **Yahweh** earlier and a pronoun later. Alternate translation: [and he kept Yahweh’s commandments, which he had commanded Moses]

7.note: The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Yahweh helped Samuel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the same expression in 1 Samuel 3:19. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [And Yahweh helped him]

The author is using **he went out** as a common expression of his culture to mean “he led his army into battle.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he went to war] or [he led his army into battle]

8.note: The author is stating the pronoun **He** separately, even though the verb translated as **he struck** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to put focus on Hezekiah as the king who led the Judean army to do this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. See how you translated the same expression in 14:7. Alternate translation: [He was the king who struck]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [he defeated the Philistines]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:32. Alternate translation: [and its territory]
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:9. Alternate translation: [conquering settlements of all sizes]

9.note: The author is using this phrase to introduce a new event. See how you translated the same phrase in [2:1](ta:02).

9.q: בַּ⁠שָּׁנָ֤ה הָֽ⁠רְבִיעִית֙ לַ⁠מֶּ֣לֶךְ חִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ הִ֚יא הַ⁠שָּׁנָ֣ה הַ⁠שְּׁבִיעִ֔ית לְ⁠הוֹשֵׁ֥עַ
9.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **fourth** or **seventh**, you could represent these number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year four of Hezekiah (it was year seven of Hoshea]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:3. Alternate translation: [came]

10.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the Assyrians. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Assyrians captured it]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:25. Alternate translation: [In the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea]

The expression **was captured** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Assyrians captured Samaria]

11.note: Here, **Israel** represents the Israelites. Since the author uses the plural pronoun **them** for the Israelites in the next sentence, it may be helpful to use a plural term here. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

12.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. The author does not mean that the king of Assyria did the things he described in the previous verse because of the things he describes in this verse. He is explaining that the things in the previous verse happened because of the things in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. The UST models one way to do that.
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:6. Alternate translation: [they did not listen to what Yahweh their God had told them to do]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:6. Alternate translation: [they did not obey what Yahweh their God had told them to do]

Since, in this context, the term **listen** means “obey,” these two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and they did not obey him at all]

13.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:25. Alternate translation: [And in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah]

The author is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. It becomes clear in the next verse, understood in light of 19:8, that there were some significant cities that Sennacherib had not yet captured. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and he captured one after another] or [and he captured many of them]

14.note: Hezekiah is speaking as if he had actually **sinned** or done something that was against Yahweh’s commandments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have done the wrong thing by not serving you]

Hezekiah is speaking as if he were actually a beast of burden and would **bear** a load that Sennacherib would put on him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Whatever you impose on me, I will pay]

14.q: שְׁלֹ֤שׁ מֵאוֹת֙ כִּכַּר־כֶּ֔סֶף וּ⁠שְׁלֹשִׁ֖ים כִּכַּ֥ר זָהָֽב
14.note: See how you decided to represent the weight of a kikkar in 5:5.

15.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 12:18. Alternate translation: [that was]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:18. Alternate translation: [in the temple of Yahweh]

16.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [cut off the gold from the doors of the temple of Yahweh and the doorposts]
Since the author has already used Hezekiah’s name earlier in this sentence, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun here. Alternate translation: [that he had overlaid]

The pronoun **them** refers to the gold that Hezekiah **cut off** from the doors and doorposts of the temple. In some languages it may be more natural to use a singular pronoun to represent this gold, particularly if it might otherwise seem that Hezekiah sent the doors and doorposts to the king of Assyria. Alternate translation: [and he gave it]

17.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֣ח & אֶת־תַּרְתָּ֥ן וְ⁠אֶת־רַב־סָרִ֣יס ׀ וְ⁠אֶת־רַב־שָׁקֵ֨ה מִן־לָכִ֜ישׁ אֶל־הַ⁠מֶּ֧לֶךְ חִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ בְּ⁠חֵ֥יל כָּבֵ֖ד יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם
17.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the **heavy army** with the information about the officials whom the Assyrian king sent, and the information that he sent them **{to} Jerusalem** with the information that he sent them **from Lachish**. Alternate translation: [sent the Tartan and the Rabsaris and the Rabshakeh with a heavy army from Lachish {to} Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah]

The terms **Tartan**, **Rabsaris**, and **Rabshakeh** are Assyrian words, titles of important officials, that the biblical author is using in his account and spelling the way they sound in his language. You could do the same thing, or you could translate the meaning of each term into your language. If you use the Assyrian words, you could explain what they mean in a footnote. Alternate translation: [his supreme commander, his chief officer, and his field commander]

17.q: וַֽ⁠יַּעֲלוּ֙ וַ⁠יָּבֹ֣אוּ יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם וַ⁠יַּעֲל֣וּ וַ⁠יָּבֹ֗אוּ וַ⁠יַּֽעַמְדוּ֙
17.note: The author is repeating the statement **And they went up, and they came** for stylistic purposes. The repetition illustrates and dramatizes the steady advance of the Assyrian army up the mountain slopes to the city of Jerusalem. It allows readers to share in the suspense and dread that the people of Jerusalem felt as this army approached. If a storyteller in your language would not repeat a statement in this way, you may be able to achieve the same effects in your translation in some other way. Alternate translation: [And the Assyrians advanced inexorably up the mountain slopes to the city of Jerusalem, finally stopping]

19.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵ⁠הֶם֙ רַב־שָׁקֵ֔ה אִמְרוּ־נָ֖א אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר הַ⁠מֶּ֤לֶךְ הַ⁠גָּדוֹל֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר מָ֧ה הַ⁠בִּטָּח֛וֹן הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּטָֽחְתָּ
19.note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the multiple levels of quotation in verses 19–25. There are three levels of quotation in this verse. The author is quoting what **the Rabshakeh** said (level 1). The Rabshakeh tells Hezekiah’s officials what he wants them to say **to Hezekiah** (level 2). This includes a quotation from **the king of Assyria** (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

19.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵ⁠הֶם֙ רַב־שָׁקֵ֔ה אִמְרוּ־נָ֖א אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר הַ⁠מֶּ֤לֶךְ הַ⁠גָּדוֹל֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר מָ֧ה הַ⁠בִּטָּח֛וֹן הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּטָֽחְתָּ
19.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, starting in this verse. Alternate translation: [And the Rabshakeh told them, “Tell Hezekiah that the great king, the king of Assyria, wants to know what this trust is that he is trusting]

The implied “you” in the imperative **say** is plural here because the Rabshakeh is addressing all three of Hezekiah’s officials. So use the plural form here in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The word **you** is singular here because the king of Assyria (speaking through the Rabshakeh) is addressing Hezekiah directly. The words “you” and “yourself” are singular in verses 20 and 21 for the same reason. So use singular forms in these verses in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The king of Assyria is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [What is this trust that you have] or [In whom are you trusting]

The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one in whom you can trust to protect you from us!]

20.q: אָמַ֨רְתָּ֙ אַךְ־דְּבַר־שְׂפָתַ֔יִם עֵצָ֥ה וּ⁠גְבוּרָ֖ה לַ⁠מִּלְחָמָ֑ה עַתָּה֙ עַל־מִ֣י בָטַ֔חְתָּ כִּ֥י מָרַ֖דְתָּ בִּֽ⁠י
20.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The great king says that he is only speaking a word of lips when he says that he has counsel and might for war. The king asks in whom he is trusting, that he rebels against him.]

This could mean: (1) that the Assyrian king is saying Hezekiah claims to have sufficient military strength and strategy to resist, but that is mere talk. The ULT follows this interpretation. Alternate translation: [When you say, ‘I have counsel and might for war,’ that is just a word of lips] or (2) that the king is contrasting brave talk with what is actually needed for war. In that case, he would not be quoting Hezekiah. Alternate translation: [All you have is mere talk. Counsel and might are actually needed for war]

There is a fourth level of quotation here, in addition to the three that a note describes in the previous verse. According to the interpretation that the ULT follows, the king of Assyria (level 3), whom Hezekiah’s officials are to quote (level 2), as the Rabshakeh tells them to do (level 1), is quoting what he believes Hezekiah is saying (level 4). If you have decided to mark levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate punctuation in your language for this level as well.

The king of Assyria is using **a word of lips** as a common expression of his culture to mean “mere talk.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You speak only empty words] or [It is mere talk when you say]

20.q: עַתָּה֙ עַל־מִ֣י בָטַ֔חְתָּ כִּ֥י מָרַ֖דְתָּ בִּֽ⁠י
20.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one you can trust to help you, that you should rebel against me]

21.q: עַתָּ֡ה הִנֵּ֣ה בָטַ֣חְתָּ לְּ⁠ךָ֡ עַל־מִשְׁעֶנֶת֩ הַ⁠קָּנֶ֨ה הָ⁠רָצ֤וּץ הַ⁠זֶּה֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִסָּמֵ֥ךְ אִישׁ֙ עָלָ֔י⁠ו וּ⁠בָ֥א בְ⁠כַפּ֖⁠וֹ וּ⁠נְקָבָ֑⁠הּ כֵּ֚ן פַּרְעֹ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ־מִצְרַ֔יִם לְ⁠כָֽל־הַ⁠בֹּטְחִ֖ים עָלָֽי⁠ו
21.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The great king says that behold, Hezekiah is trusting in Egypt to help him, but that is like using a broken reed as a staff. If a man leans on it, it goes into his palm and pierces it. That is what Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is like for anyone who trusts in him]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:9.

21.q: בָטַ֣חְתָּ לְּ⁠ךָ֡ עַל־מִשְׁעֶנֶת֩ הַ⁠קָּנֶ֨ה הָ⁠רָצ֤וּץ הַ⁠זֶּה֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם
21.note: The king of Assyria is speaking as if **Egypt** were actually a **broken reed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you believe that you can rely on Egypt, but that is like using a broken reed as a staff]

The king of Assyria is using the possessive form to describe a **staff** that consists of a **broken reed**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in this broken reed, Egypt, as a staff]

22.q: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמְר֣וּ⁠ן אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֣חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲו֖וּ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
22.note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form to challenge the claim that Hezekiah’s officials might make that they are trusting in Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And you should not say to me, ‘We trust in Yahweh our God,’ since he is the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, ‘To the face of this altar in Jerusalem you shall prostrate yourselves’!]

22.q: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמְר֣וּ⁠ן אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֣חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲו֖וּ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
22.note: The second-level and third-level quotations that began in verse 19 conclude at the end of verse 21. There are two levels of quotation in this verse. The Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah’s officials directly (level 1), and he quotes what the officials might say and what Hezekiah has said (level 2). If you have been marking levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate punctuation in your language for the levels in this verse.

22.q: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמְר֣וּ⁠ן אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֣חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲו֖וּ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
22.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The great king says that Hezekiah should not tell him that you Judeans are trusting in Yahweh your God. After all, he is the one whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah has removed and told the people of Judah and Jerusalem that they must prostrate themselves to the face of the altar in Jerusalem.]

The word **you** is plural in the first instance because the Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah’s three officials. The word **you** in the second instance and the word **yourself** are plural because Hezekiah was addressing all of the Judeans. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

By **We**, Hezekiah’s officials would mean themselves and their fellow Judeans but not the Rabshakeh, to whom they would be speaking. So use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, **Judah** and **Jerusalem** represent the people who live in those places. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people of Judah and Jerusalem]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:12. Alternate translation: [In front of]

23.q: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הִתְעָ֣רֶב נָ֔א אֶת־אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י אֶת־מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְ⁠אֶתְּנָ֤ה לְ⁠ךָ֙ אַלְפַּ֣יִם סוּסִ֔ים אִם־תּוּכַ֕ל לָ֥⁠תֶת לְ⁠ךָ֖ רֹכְבִ֥ים עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם
23.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [And now, please invite Hezekiah to make a wager with my master, the king of Assyria. Tell him that I will give him 2,000 horses if he is able to put riders on them for himself]

This is the beginning of something that the Rabshakeh is saying directly to Hezekiah. He implicitly wants the Judean officials to quote to Hezekiah what he says. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this in your translation. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah from me, ‘And now]

**And now** was an expression that speakers in this culture commonly used to introduce an important point such as the implications of what they were just saying. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. See how you translated this expression in 3:23.

The implied “you” in the imperative **wager** and the pronouns **you** and **yourself** are singular in each instance because the Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah directly. The words “you” and “yourself” are singular in verse 24 for the same reason. So use singular forms in these verses in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

24.q: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְּטַנִּ֑ים וַ⁠תִּבְטַ֤ח לְ⁠ךָ֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם לְ⁠רֶ֖כֶב וּ⁠לְ⁠פָרָשִֽׁים
24.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [But ask him how he would turn back the face of a captain of one of the least servants of my master. Tell him I know that is why he is trusting for himself in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen]

24.q: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְּטַנִּ֑ים
24.note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But even then, you would not be able to turn back the face of a captain of one of the least servants of my master!]

24.q: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְּטַנִּ֑ים
24.note: The Rabshakeh is using one part of a person, his **face**, to mean all of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But how would you turn back a captain of one of the least servants of my master] or [But how would you force a captain to retreat even if he was one of the least servants of my master]

The Rabshakeh is using the possessive form to describe a **captain** who would be **one of the least servants** of the king of Assyria, that is, one of his weakest soldiers. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a captain who was among the least servants of my master]

This is the end of what the Rabshakeh is saying directly to Hezekiah. In the next verse, the Rabshakeh quotes the end of the message from Sennacherib that he wants the officials to give to Hezekiah. If you have been marking levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate closing punctuation at the end of this verse.

25.q: עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לְ⁠הַשְׁחִת֑⁠וֹ יְהוָה֙ אָמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י עֲלֵ֛ה עַל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את וְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָֽ⁠הּ
25.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah that the king of Assyria says that he has not come up against this place to destroy it without Yahweh. Yahweh told him to go up against this land and destroy it]

25.q: עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לְ⁠הַשְׁחִת֑⁠וֹ יְהוָה֙ אָמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י עֲלֵ֛ה עַל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את וְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָֽ⁠הּ
25.note: There are four levels of quotation in this verse. If you have decided to mark levels of quotation with punctuation, see what you did in the similar case of the four levels in verses 19 and 20.

25.q: עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לְ⁠הַשְׁחִת֑⁠וֹ
25.note: This is the beginning of something that Sennacherib is saying directly to Hezekiah. It is the rest of the message that the Rabshakeh began to quote in verses 19–21. The Rabshakeh implicitly wants the Judean officials to quote this to Hezekiah as something that Sennacherib has said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this in your translation. Alternate translation: [Say to Hezekiah, ‘Thus says the great king, “Now have I come up]

25.q: עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לְ⁠הַשְׁחִת֑⁠וֹ
25.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not think that I have come up against this place to destroy it without Yahweh!]

Sennacherib is not using the phrase **without Yahweh** to mean that Hezekiah should not think that he has come without Yahweh accompanying him. Rather, he means that he has come after receiving a command from Yahweh. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [without receiving a command to do so from Yahweh]

26.note: Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah are speaking of themselves in the third person as **your servants** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to us, your servants,]

26.q: דַּבֶּר־נָ֤א אֶל־עֲבָדֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ אֲרָמִ֔ית כִּ֥י שֹׁמְעִ֖ים אֲנָ֑חְנוּ
26.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since we, your servants, understand Aramaic, please speak to us in that language]

Eliakim is using the name of the dialect of Hebrew that people spoke in the kingdom of Judah. Some versions use the name of the language rather than the name of this dialect and say “in Hebrew.” If you have decided to use the same names in your translation that the biblical author does, you may wish to use the name Judean here. If not, you may wish to use the name Hebrew here.

Here, **ears** represent “hearing.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the hearing of the people who are on the wall] or [, since the people who are on the wall can hear us]

27.q: הַ⁠עַ֨ל אֲדֹנֶ֤י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אֵלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ שְׁלָחַ֣⁠נִי אֲדֹנִ֔⁠י לְ⁠דַבֵּ֖ר אֶת־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֣ים הָ⁠אֵ֑לֶּה הֲ⁠לֹ֣א עַל־הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֗ים הַ⁠יֹּֽשְׁבִים֙ עַל־הַ֣⁠חֹמָ֔ה לֶ⁠אֱכֹ֣ל אֶת חרי⁠הם וְ⁠לִ⁠שְׁתּ֛וֹת אֶת־שיני⁠הם עִמָּ⁠כֶֽם
27.note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [My master did not send me to speak these words only to your master and to you! He also sent me to speak them to the men sitting on the wall, who will eat their dung and drink their urine with you!]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:7. Alternate translation: [this message]

Even though the author says that the Rabshakeh spoke to **them**, the word **your** and the word **you** in its first instance are singular because the Rabshakeh is replying directly to Eliakim, who spoke on behalf of all three Judean officials. The word **you** in its second instance is plural because the Rabshakeh is including Shebnah and Joah in what he says will happen. Use the appropriate singular and plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

28.note: The author probably does not mean that the Rabshakeh had been sitting down and having a private conversation with the Judean officials and that he then **stood** up. If the conversation had been private, there would have been no need for Eliakim to ask him to speak in Aramaic so that the people on the wall would not understand. So the author probably means that the Rabshakeh stood in such a way that his speech to the people on the wall would seem even more forceful and intimidating. Alternate translation: [And the Rabshakeh assumed a dominating stance]
See how you decided at 1:10 to represent the phrase **and said** when it introduces a direct quotation.

29.q: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ אַל־יַשִּׁ֥יא לָ⁠כֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּי־לֹ֣א יוּכַ֔ל לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם מִ⁠יָּדֽ⁠וֹ
29.note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the multiple levels of quotation in verses 19–25. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate all of this long quotation so that there are not quotations within quotations. Alternate translation: [The king says that you should not let Hezekiah deceive you, since he is not able to deliver you from his hand]

29.q: אַל־יַשִּׁ֥יא לָ⁠כֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּי־לֹ֣א יוּכַ֔ל לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם מִ⁠יָּדֽ⁠וֹ
29.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “his hand.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “my hand.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

29.q: אַל־יַשִּׁ֥יא לָ⁠כֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּי־לֹ֣א יוּכַ֔ל לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם מִ⁠יָּדֽ⁠וֹ
29.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since Hezekiah is not able to deliver you from my hand, do not let him deceive you]

The word **you** is plural in both of these instances because king of Assyria, speaking through the Rabshakeh, is addressing the Judeans who have gathered on the city wall. For the same reason, the words “you” and “your” and the implied “you” in imperatives are also plural throughout verses 30–32. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

30.q: וְ⁠אַל־יַבְטַ֨ח אֶתְ⁠כֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר הַצֵּ֥ל יַצִּילֵ֖⁠נוּ יְהוָ֑ה וְ⁠לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ אֶת־הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
30.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what the Rabshakeh said (level 1), continuing from the previous verse. The Rabshakeh is quoting the king of Assyria (level 2), also continuing from the previous verse. The king is quoting Hezekiah (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

30.q: וְ⁠אַל־יַבְטַ֨ח אֶתְ⁠כֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר הַצֵּ֥ל יַצִּילֵ֖⁠נוּ יְהוָ֑ה וְ⁠לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ אֶת־הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
30.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The king says that you should not let Hezekiah make you trust in Yahweh by telling you that delivering, Yahweh will deliver all of you, and this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria]

According to the king of Assyria, Hezekiah has been repeating forms of the verb **deliver** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will certainly deliver us]
By **us**, Hezekiah means to include both himself and those to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction, here and in verse 32.

The expression **will not be given** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will not give this city]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:10. Alternate translation: [into the control of]

31.note: To translate the term “listen” here and in the next verse, see how you translated the similar expression in 10:6. Alternate translation: [Do not do what Hezekiah wants you to do here]

31.q: כִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֜ר מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֗וּר עֲשֽׂוּ־אִתִּ֤⁠י בְרָכָה֙ וּ⁠צְא֣וּ אֵלַ֔⁠י וְ⁠אִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ־גַּפְנ⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵֽנָת֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵֽי־בוֹרֽ⁠וֹ
31.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [the king of Assyria is telling you to make a blessing with him and come out to him. Then you will be able to eat, a man of his vine and a man of his fig tree, and drink, a man from the waters of his well]

Here, **a blessing**, meaning a gift, represents “a peace agreement,” since in this culture people exchanged gifts when they made peace agreements. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Make a peace agreement with me]

31.q: וְ⁠אִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ־גַּפְנ⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵֽנָת֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵֽי־בוֹרֽ⁠וֹ
31.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:23. Alternate translation: [and let each of you eat from his vine and fig tree, and let each of you drink from the waters of his well]

32.q: עַד־בֹּאִ⁠י֩ וְ⁠לָקַחְתִּ֨י אֶתְ⁠כֶ֜ם אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּ⁠אַרְצְ⁠כֶ֗ם אֶרֶץ֩ דָּגָ֨ן וְ⁠תִיר֜וֹשׁ אֶ֧רֶץ לֶ֣חֶם וּ⁠כְרָמִ֗ים אֶ֣רֶץ זֵ֤ית יִצְהָר֙ וּ⁠דְבַ֔שׁ וִֽ⁠חְי֖וּ וְ⁠לֹ֣א תָמֻ֑תוּ וְ⁠אַֽל־תִּשְׁמְעוּ֙ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ כִּֽי־יַסִּ֤ית אֶתְ⁠כֶם֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר יְהוָ֖ה יַצִּילֵֽ⁠נוּ
32.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what the Rabshakeh said (level 1), continuing from the previous verse. The Rabshakeh is quoting the king of Assyria (level 2), also continuing from the previous verse. The king is quoting Hezekiah (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

32.q: עַד־בֹּאִ⁠י֩ וְ⁠לָקַחְתִּ֨י אֶתְ⁠כֶ֜ם אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּ⁠אַרְצְ⁠כֶ֗ם אֶרֶץ֩ דָּגָ֨ן וְ⁠תִיר֜וֹשׁ אֶ֧רֶץ לֶ֣חֶם וּ⁠כְרָמִ֗ים אֶ֣רֶץ זֵ֤ית יִצְהָר֙ וּ⁠דְבַ֔שׁ וִֽ⁠חְי֖וּ וְ⁠לֹ֣א תָמֻ֑תוּ וְ⁠אַֽל־תִּשְׁמְעוּ֙ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ כִּֽי־יַסִּ֤ית אֶתְ⁠כֶם֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר יְהוָ֖ה יַצִּילֵֽ⁠נוּ
32.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [until he comes and takes you to a land like your land, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive of oil and honey. He tells you to live and not die. He says that you should not listen to Hezekiah when he misleads you by telling you that Yahweh will deliver all of you]
Since the rest of the items on this list are agricultural products, these **vineyards** may represent the products of vineyards. Alternate translation: [and grapes]

The phrase **olive of oil** describes cultivated olives, that is, olives from trees in orchards as opposed to wild olives, which yielded less and worse oil. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [cultivated olives]

33.q: הַ⁠הַצֵּ֥ל הִצִּ֛ילוּ אֱלֹהֵ֥י הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֖ם אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־אַרְצ֑⁠וֹ מִ⁠יַּ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
33.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [None of the gods of the nations actually delivered the land where people worshiped it from the hand of the king of Assyria!]

33.q: הַ⁠הַצֵּ֥ל הִצִּ֛ילוּ אֱלֹהֵ֥י הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֖ם אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־אַרְצ֑⁠וֹ מִ⁠יַּ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
33.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The king tells you to consider that none of the gods of the nations has delivered its land from the hand of the king of Assyria]

The king is repeating forms of the verb **deliver** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Did the gods of the nations actually deliver]

The king is not suggesting that each of these **gods** is a **man** at best. He is using a common expression of this culture. See how you translated the similar expressions in 3:23 and, in this context, 18:31. Alternate translation: [did the gods of the nations deliver, any of them, its land] or [did any of the gods of the nations deliver its land]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:10. Alternate translation: [from the power of the king of Assyria and similarly in the next two verses]

The king of Assyria is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making a triumphant declaration. (The expression “my hand” in verses 34 and 35 is equivalent in this context.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [from my hand]

34.q: אַיֵּה֩ אֱלֹהֵ֨י חֲמָ֜ת וְ⁠אַרְפָּ֗ד אַיֵּ֛ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י סְפַרְוַ֖יִם הֵנַ֣ע וְ⁠עִוָּ֑ה כִּֽי־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־שֹׁמְר֖וֹן מִ⁠יָּדִֽ⁠י
34.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [The gods of Hamath and Arpad did nothing to help those people! The gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah did nothing to help those people! Indeed, the gods of Samaria did not deliver it from my hand!]

34.q: אַיֵּה֩ אֱלֹהֵ֨י חֲמָ֜ת וְ⁠אַרְפָּ֗ד אַיֵּ֛ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י סְפַרְוַ֖יִם הֵנַ֣ע וְ⁠עִוָּ֑ה כִּֽי־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־שֹׁמְר֖וֹן מִ⁠יָּדִֽ⁠י
34.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The king points out that the gods of Hamath and Arpad did nothing to help those people, and the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah did nothing to help those people, and in fact the gods of Samaria did not deliver it from his hand]

The pronoun **they** does not refer to the gods that the king has just listed. It refers generally back to “the gods of the nations” in the previous verse and specifically to the gods that the people of the kingdom of Israel, called **Samaria** here, were worshiping. Alternate translation: [did the gods of Samaria deliver it]

35.q: מִ֚י בְּ⁠כָל־אֱלֹהֵ֣י הָֽ⁠אֲרָצ֔וֹת אֲשֶׁר־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־אַרְצָ֖⁠ם מִ⁠יָּדִ֑⁠י כִּי־יַצִּ֧יל יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם מִ⁠יָּדִֽ⁠י
35.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form to emphasize that none of the gods of other nations have been able to rescue their lands from the Assyrian king. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You cannot name any of the gods of the lands that have delivered their land from my hand, so do not believe that Yahweh will deliver Jerusalem from my hand!]

35.q: מִ֚י בְּ⁠כָל־אֱלֹהֵ֣י הָֽ⁠אֲרָצ֔וֹת אֲשֶׁר־הִצִּ֥ילוּ אֶת־אַרְצָ֖⁠ם מִ⁠יָּדִ֑⁠י כִּי־יַצִּ֧יל יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם מִ⁠יָּדִֽ⁠י
35.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there would not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The king emphasizes that none of the gods of the lands have delivered their lands from his hand, so you should not believe that Yahweh will deliver Jerusalem from his hand]

In this instance, the word **land** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the lands where these **gods** were worshiped. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “land.” Alternate translation: [their lands]

36.q: וְ⁠הֶחֱרִ֣ישׁוּ הָ⁠עָ֔ם וְ⁠לֹֽא־עָנ֥וּ אֹת֖⁠וֹ דָּבָ֑ר כִּי־מִצְוַ֨ת הַ⁠מֶּ֥לֶךְ הִ֛יא לֵ⁠אמֹ֖ר לֹ֥א תַעֲנֻֽ⁠הוּ
36.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [But since it was a commandment of the king, saying, “You shall not answer him,” the people were silent and did not answer him a word]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [But the people said nothing in response to him]

37.note: The expression **torn** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [tore their clothes and came to Hezekiah]
See how you indicated the symbolic significance of this action in 2:12.
